title: Rosalind and the Room
premise: Ivo Crane, a nonbinary urban explorer who documents forgotten spaces as a way of proving they exist, discovers an unmapped tunnel beneath their late grandmother's house—and realizes the photographs they took there years ago have changed: every image now contains an extra chair, and in the newest ones, someone is almost sitting in it. The room belongs to Rosalind, a woman erased from the town's records after a century-old injustice, who has been waiting for someone willing to witness her. As frost creeps through the house in patterns that spell out the verses of a song Rosalind once sang with the condemned, Ivo must learn the song's final verse—without singing along, which would bind them to the room forever—and carry her name back into the world of the living. In the end, Ivo chooses visibility over safety, testifying to what they've documented, and Rosalind's chair is finally empty because she is finally remembered.
about_author: Paloma Blackwood is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed estate photographs before turning to horror. They write about the violence of being undocumented and the ghosts that paperwork leaves behind.

chapters.title: The Survey That Isn't
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. While mapping storm drains under the old mill district, Ivo finds a passage that appears on no survey, no deed, no memory—a gap in the record that feels personal. The emotional beat is the thrill of discovery curdling into recognition: Ivo knows what it means to be left off the map.

chapters.title: Grandma's House, Annotated
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Clearing out their grandmother's house, Ivo re-examines old photographs for the estate inventory and finds an extra wooden chair in every shot from 1998 onward—furniture that was never there. The beat is quiet dread; documentation, Ivo's form of prayer, has started answering back.

chapters.title: Frost Writing
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Overnight frost blooms on the windows in repeating patterns—lines of a song, half-legible. A neighbor mentions the house 'always did belong to the Crane girl who drowned,' though no such girl exists in any record. The beat is the first intrusion of the past into the present tense.

chapters.title: Rosalind
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV, shifting briefly to Rosalind's fragmented voice in italics. Following the tunnel from the mill district, Ivo surfaces inside the house's sealed root cellar, where a woman sits in the extra chair, patient as furniture. She says only: 'You brought the camera. Good. Someone should remember correctly.' The beat is terror meeting terrible courtesy.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Left Out
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Researching county archives, Ivo reconstructs Rosalind Crane's erasure: in 1923 she testified against the mill owners' fatal negligence, was declared insane, committed, and struck from family records—the song was what the workers sang at her hearing. The beat is righteous anger; injustice didn't just kill her, it edited her.

chapters.title: Three Verses and a Warning
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Rosalind teaches Ivo the song's first three verses, each one etching itself deeper into the frost and into Ivo's dreams. She warns: learn the last verse but never sing it aloud, or you'll take her seat permanently. The beat is intimacy shadowed by trap—Ivo is beginning to care about her.

chapters.title: The Chair Moves Closer
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. The chair begins appearing in rooms Ivo occupies outside the house—in their apartment photos, in a café window reflection. Frost follows them. Ivo realizes Rosalind isn't haunting them; the erasure is, dragging witnesses toward the room. The beat is claustrophobic escalation.

chapters.title: Everyone Who Sang Along
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Ivo and archival letters. Ivo finds the fates of others who learned the song: a folklorist in 1961, a cousin in 1987—all vanished mid-verse, all chairs now accounted for. Rosalind confesses she never asked them to stay; the room did. The beat is grief and the question of whether helping her damns everyone.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. On the winter solstice, with frost covering every window, Ivo enters the room to hear the final verse—the names of every worker the mill killed, sung so they can be carried out. Rosalind holds the melody; Ivo must listen without joining, while the room pulls at their throat like drowning. The climax: Ivo stays silent, memorizes everything, and walks out as the chair cracks behind them.

chapters.title: Read Into the Record
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Ivo publishes the full documentation—the tunnel, the ledger, the song, Rosalind's testimony—at a public hearing on the mill site's redevelopment, speaking her name into the official record. The frost stops; the chair appears in one last photograph, empty, by an open door. The beat is hard-won belonging: Ivo was seen witnessing, and that was enough to free her.
